title: Final: paths and space
sub: New problems to recognise, Union-Find on the rig, a grid trap, the cost of Dijkstra, and an answer to "pathfinding for 500 units"
cards/0/q: Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid (#1368, hard). A grid of up to 100 × 100 with an arrow in every cell: right, left, down or up. Following an arrow is free; turning a cell's arrow costs 1. Find the cheapest path from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one. What is it?
cards/0/options/0: 0-1 BFS: a step along the arrow is a 0-edge to the front of the deque, any other step a 1-edge to the back
cards/0/options/1: BFS by levels: fewer steps means cheaper
cards/0/options/2: A* with Manhattan: there is one known goal
cards/0/explain: Every step out of a cell costs 0 (along the arrow) or 1 (against it) — weights of only 0 and 1. 0-1 BFS gives O(V + E) ≈ 5·10⁴ operations; Dijkstra is correct too, but with an extra log.
cards/0/wrong/1: The number of steps is not the cost here: a long path along arrows is free, while a short one may need turns.
cards/0/wrong/2: Manhattan estimates steps, but the cost is turns: a 10-step path may cost 0. Such an h overestimates, and A* loses its guarantee.
cards/1/q: Path with Maximum Probability (#1514). An undirected graph of up to 10⁴ vertices and 2·10⁴ edges; each edge has a probability of getting across, from 0 to 1. Find the path from start to end with the highest probability — the product over its edges. What do you use?
cards/1/options/0: Dijkstra in reverse: a max-heap by probability, a product instead of a sum
cards/1/options/1: BFS: a path with fewer edges is more likely
cards/1/explain: Probabilities are ≤ 1, so extending a path never increases the product — exactly the "path cost is monotone" property Dijkstra rests on, only mirrored: the highest probability popped is final. O(E log V).
cards/1/wrong/1: Two edges of 0.9 give 0.81, while one edge of 0.5 gives less. The number of edges decides nothing.
cards/1/wrong/2: Bellman–Ford is correct but O(V·E) = 2·10⁸, and fractional weights do not bother Dijkstra: all it needs is monotonicity.
cards/2/q: Path With Maximum Minimum Value (#1102). A grid of up to 100 × 100 numbers from 0 to 10⁹. The score of a path from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one is the smallest number on it. Find the largest score. What fits best?
cards/2/options/0: Union-Find: add cells in decreasing order of value until the corners share a group
cards/2/options/1: A*: there is one goal and a geometric estimate of the distance to it
cards/2/options/2: Dijkstra over the sum of cell values
cards/2/explain: This is the mirror of the minimax from the lesson on the path with the smallest maximum: maximise the worst cell. Union-Find in decreasing order — the answer is the cell after which the corners connect; Dijkstra with a max-heap and min instead of max works too, and so does binary search on the answer with BFS.
cards/2/wrong/1: The distance to the goal is irrelevant here: a path's cost is its worst cell, not its length.
cards/2/wrong/2: A sum of values is not the score: a path with a large sum may pass through a single cell holding zero.
cards/3/q: A shooter: 300 bots on a NavMesh, each with its own patrol point, paths recomputed every 2 seconds. How do you set it up?
cards/3/options/0: A* over the NavMesh for each bot, with the recomputations spread across frames
cards/3/options/1: A flow field for every patrol point
cards/3/options/2: One flow field for all the bots
cards/3/explain: Every bot has a different goal — a field cannot be shared. 300 searches every 2 seconds is 150 per second, which at 60 FPS is 2–3 searches per frame if they are queued. A search over NavMesh polygons is short.
cards/3/wrong/1: 300 fields over the whole map for 300 different goals is 300 full Dijkstras instead of 300 short A* searches.
cards/3/wrong/2: A field leads to its goals. One field from all 300 points leads each bot to the nearest point, not to its own.
cards/4/task: Redundant Connection (#684): a graph of n vertices was a tree, and one extra edge was added; return an edge that can be removed, and if there are several, the last one in the input. Step through Union-Find over the edges: path compression and union by rank. The rig asks what happens on edge 4-5.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: The ranks are equal: one tree goes under the other, and the root's rank grows
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: The roots match: edge 4-5 is redundant
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Edge 4-5: find(4) went 4 → 3 → 1, and 5 is its own root. Root 1 has rank 2, root 5 has rank 1. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: The roots differ — 4 and 5 were not connected yet, so the edge is needed. The ranks are not equal: the shorter tree (root 5, rank 1) goes under the taller one (root 1, rank 2), and the height does not grow — rank[1] stays 2. The redundant edge turns out to be 2-6: by then 2 and 6 share root 1.
cards/5/q: #1828 with a grid. On circles with r = 4 this code counts fewer points than brute force. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/5/explain: A 3 × 3 square covers the circle only if a cell is no smaller than the radius. With r = 4 the cell came out as 2, and a point 4 units from the centre lies one cell further out — the code never reads its bucket. Either size = max r, or read 5 × 5 cells: as many as it takes to cover the radius.
cards/6/q: Dijkstra with lazy deletion on a 1000 × 1000 grid, 4 neighbours. How many entries can the heap hold in the worst case, and what is the complexity?
cards/6/options/0: Up to ≈ 4·10⁶ — one per successful relaxation; O(E log V)
cards/6/options/1: At most 10⁶ — one entry per cell
cards/6/options/2: Up to 10¹² — every cell with every cell
cards/6/explain: Every successful relaxation pushes an entry, and there are no more of those than directed edges, E ≈ 4V = 4·10⁶. A heap operation is O(log E) = O(log V), and altogether it is O(E log V) ≈ 4·10⁶ · 22 ≈ 10⁸.
cards/6/wrong/1: One entry per cell is a heap with decrease-key, or a flow field where the cost sits on the cell. With lazy deletion a cell is pushed on every improvement.
cards/6/wrong/2: Entries only come from edges, and a cell has 4 of them: up to 4·10⁶, not V².
cards/7/q: A Unity interview: "Build pathfinding for 500 units in an RTS". Put the steps of your answer in order.
cards/7/items/0: Clarify: grid or NavMesh, one goal per group or different ones, how often the map changes
cards/7/items/1: Baseline: A* per unit — 500 searches, estimate their cost per frame
cards/7/items/2: A shared goal for a group — one flow field: Dijkstra from the goal and an arrow per cell
cards/7/items/3: Different goals — A* with a good h, searches spread over frames or moved into Jobs
cards/7/items/4: The crowd: local avoidance, with neighbours found by a spatial grid
cards/7/items/5: Cost: a field rebuild in O(V log V) on events, O(1) per unit per frame
cards/7/items/6: Edge cases: an unreachable goal, cut-off cells, the player blocking the path
cards/7/explain: The key is to ask about goals first: that decides between A* and a field. Then an honest baseline, the choice, the crowd and the cost. Edge cases at the end show you have done this in a real game.

cards/8/pairs/1/1: Dijkstra with max instead of a sum
cards/8/pairs/2/0: One goal, a different one per unit (#1091)
